title: Confessions close
hook: an apology that lands does two things at once; Augustine named his whole book after that double move
tomorrow: what makes a little book for beginners worth carrying for life?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last page: the seventh day with no evening, and a rest in God that doesn't end. The line was a sabbath without evening.

An apology that's all excuses doesn't land. Neither does one that's all groveling. The kind that lands does two things at once: here's what I did, and here's what you mean to me. Augustine named his whole book after that double move. It's why the Confessions doesn't open with a sin. It opens, in the Pusey translation, like this: "Great art Thou, O Lord, and greatly to be praised." Today the book closes, on its own title.
screen: `NOT ALL EXCUSE, NOT ALL GROVELING.` → `WHAT I DID, WHAT YOU MEAN.` → `GREAT ART THOU, O LORD.`

segments.voice: In Augustine's Latin, confessio does two jobs. It means owning up: this is what I did. And it means giving glory: this is who you are. You can hear both in the Latin psalms he prayed. One psalm that opens with that verb comes into the Douay-Rheims as "Give praise to the Lord, for he is good: for his mercy endureth for ever." Confess and give praise: one verb. Looking back on the book late in life, Augustine wrote that it praises a just and good God for his bad deeds and his good ones, and stirs the reader's heart toward God. So the stolen pears aren't there to shame him. They're there so mercy can be seen. Catholic teaching still holds the two together. The Catechism calls the sacrament of penance confession because telling one's sins is at its heart, and then adds that in a deeper sense it's also a confession of God's holiness: acknowledgment and praise. Look back over the whole book: a restless heart, Monica's tears, two wills at war, a voice in a garden, a window at Ostia, the palace of memory, and a sabbath without evening. One long confession, both kinds at once.
screen: `CONFESSIO DOES TWO JOBS.` · `GIVE PRAISE TO THE LORD.` · `PRAISE FOR THE BAD AND THE GOOD.` · `THE SACRAMENT HOLDS BOTH.` · then, large: `SORROW AND PRAISE.`

segments.voice: On a scrap of paper, write one line of each. First, one thing you're sorry for, plainly, with no excuse attached. Under it, one thing you're grateful for, just as plainly, and let the two lines sit side by side.
Confession. In Augustine's Latin, both owning up to what you've done and praising who God is.
Your line: sorrow and praise. Augustine's book holds both in one long prayer, from its first page to its last. A new book opens tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholics go to confession in the sacrament of penance, naming their sins to a priest and receiving absolution. The Catechism also calls it a confession of God's holiness, an acknowledgment and praise.
